title: Client-side tokenization offload and degraded-mode strategy
content:
Purpose and high-level motivation

This note captures a proposal for performing optional client-side tokenization and an engineered degraded-mode when client tokenization is not available or fails. The goal is to reduce p99 end-to-end latency and pressure on server-side tokenizer pools for short chat requests, while preserving correct KV cache behavior and consistency for longer contexts and reruns. It also outlines how this offload interacts with KV cache semantics, kernel scheduling, and batching heuristics in the serving runtime.

Why we need this

Observed pattern: many latency-sensitive calls are small prompt completions or chat turns where the server tokenizer contributes a significant fraction of the absolute request latency, especially at p95/p99 when tokenizer pools are congested. Server-side tokenization also creates hot paths where very short requests cannot be batched effectively because they serialize on tokenizer threads.

Hypothesis: moving tokenization for well-formed client requests to the client, with a robust degraded-mode fallback on the server, can reduce tail latency and free tokenizer capacity for complex workloads. We must ensure this does not break KV cache alignment, sequence numbering, or model kernel assumptions.

Design goals

- Reduce p95/p99 end-to-end latency for single-turn and short multi-turn requests by avoiding server tokenization when safe.
- Maintain identical model input semantics between client-offloaded and server-tokenized requests so that KV cache hits are not invalidated by tokenization differences.
- Provide a safe degraded-mode on the server that can accept raw text when client tokenization is not available or untrusted.

Accepting constraints

- Clients can run different tokenizer versions and vocab variants. We cannot trust arbitrary client tokenization unless it matches the serving tokenizer variant flagged for the customer.
- KV cache keys depend on token ids and their offsets. Even tiny differences in tokenization split points cause cache misses and semantic divergence.

High-level approach

1) Tokenizer version pinning and capability negotiation
   - Each model variant in the catalog ships with a "serving tokenizer signature" string that encodes tokenizer type, vocab hash, tokenizer version, and normalization flags. Example: vocab_v13-windowed-bpe:sha256:abcd1234
   - Clients may include a headers token in the request: X-Tokenizer-Signature: <signature> and attach a pre-tokenized token id array payload instead of raw text.
   - The server validates the signature against the pinned signature for that model. If it matches, the request is treated as canonical pre-tokenized input. If not, fallback logic applies.

2) Canonical pre-tokenized request format
   - Request includes: list of integer token ids, list of token byte ranges in original text (optional), original text length, and tokenizer signature.
   - This allows the server to quickly map tokens into the KV cache and run kernels without invoking the tokenizer.

3) Degraded-mode strategies when client tokenization is absent or mismatched
   - Fast server tokenization: a lightweight, approximate tokenization path that performs conservative splitting to produce tokens that are guaranteed to be subtoken aligned with the canonical tokenizer. This path prefers over-splitting to avoid creating tokens that the canonical tokenizer would merge. Over-splitting can reduce cache hit rates but preserves semantic correctness and kernel assumptions.
   - Safe fallback to full server tokenizer when approximate path is disabled or when we detect mismatches in later validation.

4) KV cache consistency and alignment
   - The KV cache key is computed from the token ids and session id. To preserve hits, only accept client-provided tokens if signature matches exactly.
   - For approximate server tokenization we add a mapping layer: for the first time a session is tokenized by the full canonical tokenizer we record an alignment map from approximate tokens to canonical token ids. That mapping is used to rewrite previous approximate entries if a hot path is observed.

5) Batching and scheduling interactions
   - Microbatch scheduling needs to know whether incoming requests require server tokenization. Tokenization disabled requests (pre-tokenized) are eligible for immediate inference microbatching without enqueuing tokenizer executor.
   - To maximize throughput, the request scheduler maintains two queues per model variant: pre-tokenized fast lane and raw-text slow lane. The fast lane is prioritized for low latency SLO customers.
   - Tokenizer pool sizing recommendation: keep a separate lightweight pool for approximate tokenization and a full pool for canonical tokenization. Approximate pool handles high qps short requests; full pool runs less frequently.

6) Kernel and memory implications
   - Kernel execution expects contiguous token id arrays. Accepting pre-tokenized inputs allows skipping the tokenization copy stage and avoids building temporary byte buffers. This reduces memory churn and improves cache locality in the kernel path.
   - Ensure the runtime still validates token id ranges and pads to expected shapes before kernel offload.

Operational heuristics and heuristics parameters

- Eligibility rules for encouraging client offload: requests with input text length < 512 bytes and without special control tokens or streaming signals are marked client-tokenization friendly.
- Throttling when model signature rotates: if model's tokenizer signature changes during a rollout, server temporarily rejects client signatures until clients upgrade. Use a rollout grace window.
- Sampling validation: accept client pre-tokenized requests but sample 0.1% of them to re-tokenize on server and compare outputs for divergence metrics. Alert on divergence > 0.5% in tokens at positions 0..K.

Metrics to collect

- p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency split by fast-lane vs slow-lane.
- Tokenizer CPU seconds saved by client offload per model.
- KV cache hit rate delta when using pre-tokenized inputs vs server tokenization.
- Divergence rate observed during sampling.

Experimentation plan

Phase 1: internal beta with experimental client SDK feature
  - Enable header negotiation and pre-tokenized payloads in our internal SDK.
  - Route 10% of short requests to fast lane. Measure latency and divergence.

Phase 2: controlled external beta with opt-in customers
  - Expose tokenization signature to customers and allow them to opt into client-offload. Run sampling validation and monitor metrics.

Phase 3: wider rollout with enforcement and optimization
  - If divergence is low and resource savings are significant, recommend SDK default enabling for small inputs and add console toggles.

Open design questions and tradeoffs

- Should we allow clients to send token metadata like whitespace offsets? Pros: easier mapping to user-visible spans. Cons: surface for fingerprinting and privacy concerns.
- How to incentivize upstream client SDKs to keep tokenizer implementations in sync? Need release cadence and semver for tokenizer signature.
- Over-splitting approximate tokenizer reduces correctness of cache hits; we need to quantify economic tradeoff between tokenizer CPU saved and extra downstream token generation cost.

Edge cases and security considerations

- Malicious clients could craft token ids that overflow embedding tables or trigger unexpected model behavior. Always validate ids and apply per-request rate limits and syntactic checks.
- Tokenizer signatures must be cryptographically derived from the canonical tokenizer repo state and stored in model metadata.

Rollout checklist

- [ ] Implement signature negotiation server side and protocol changes in gateway
- [ ] Implement pre-tokenized payload deserialization and tight validation
- [ ] Add approximate tokenizer and light pool path
- [ ] Add sampling comparator and divergence alerting to tracing pipeline
- [ ] Update SDKs and docs, prepare migration guide for customers

Notes to reviewers

This is a pragmatic, conservative proposal aimed at improving tail latency for a common class of short requests. Key conservative element is the strict signature match required to trust client tokenization for KV cache hits. We prefer correctness over speculative cache wins in early phases. Feedback specifically requested on the approximate tokenizer behavior: prefer over-splitting or under-splitting, and thresholds for sampling divergence.

Appendix: quick pseudocode for server token acceptance

  if request.contains_pretokenized and request.signature == model.tokenizer_signature:
    validate_token_ranges(request.tokens)
    enqueue_inference_fastlane(request.tokens)
  else if request.contains_pretokenized and request.signature != model.tokenizer_signature:
    record_metric("pretoken_signature_mismatch")
    if server_config.allow_approximate_fallback:
      tokens = approximate_tokenize(request.text)
      enqueue_inference_slowlane(tokens)
    else:
      tokens = canonical_tokenize(request.text)
      enqueue_inference_slowlane(tokens)

End of document
